AP angle: the yogakshema spirit lives in the Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39, 41, 47) and in Andhra Pradesh's doorstep delivery of NTR Bharosa pensions (formerly YSR Pension Kanuka) through village and ward secretariats.

India's Constitution blends Kautilya's ideal of welfare with democratic rights and social justice, a balance that governance today must preserve and deepen.
g1m-2023-p3-6b:
Steel frameICSMerit systemAll India Services

The term "civil service" comes from the East India Company, whose covenanted servants handled civil, as distinct from military, work. Present-day Indian bureaucracy, with its district Collector, hierarchy, merit-based open competition, generalist elite and Public Service Commissions, is largely a British legacy, adapted after 1947 to a democratic Constitution. Sardar Patel called the All India Services the "steel frame" of the nation.

1. Company period (1757-1857)

  • Collector: Warren Hastings created the post of Collector in 1772, which became the pivot of district administration.
  • Lord Cornwallis (1786-93): the "father of the civil services in India" raised salaries, banned private trade and separated revenue from judicial work.
  • Covenanted services: senior posts were reserved for servants who signed covenants with the Company, almost all of them Europeans.
  • Training: Fort William College in Calcutta (1800) and Haileybury College in England (1806) trained recruits.

2. Merit and Indianisation under the Crown

  • Open competition: the Charter Act of 1853 ended patronage; the Macaulay Committee (1854) shaped the examination, first held in London in 1855.
  • First Indian: Satyendranath Tagore entered the ICS in 1863.
  • Restructuring: Lytton's Statutory Civil Service (1879) gave way, on the Aitchison Commission's (1886-87) advice, to Imperial, Provincial and Subordinate services.
  • Examinations in India: after the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms, simultaneous examinations began in 1922; the Lee Commission (1923-24) led to a Public Service Commission in 1926; the Government of India Act, 1935 created Federal and Provincial PSCs.

3. After independence

  • Continuity with change: the ICS gave way to the IAS and the Indian Police to the IPS; Sardar Patel defended them as essential for unity.
  • Constitutional base: Article 312 (All India Services), Articles 315-323 (UPSC and State PSCs) and the All India Services Act, 1951.
  • Reforms: the Kothari Committee (1976) shaped the present three-stage examination; the Second ARC (2008) and Mission Karmayogi (2020) shifted focus to performance and capacity.

4. Continuities and changes

  • Continuities: hierarchy, generalist dominance, the Collector's central role, rule-bound procedure and secrecy are colonial inheritances.
  • Changes: the services now serve elected governments, focus on development and welfare rather than revenue and order, and have become socially diverse through reservation under Article 16(4).

AP angle: the Madras Service Commission (1929), the first provincial commission, also served the Andhra region; the APPSC was formed in 1956 under Article 315.

The colonial legacy of control must now yield to a citizen-centric, accountable service, moving, in Mission Karmayogi's words, from rule to role.
g1m-2023-p3-7a:
Atmanirbhar BharatSelf-reliancePLI schemesGlobal value chains

The Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan was announced on 12 May 2020, amid COVID-19, with a special economic package of about ₹20 lakh crore (around 10% of GDP). It seeks self-reliance by building domestic capacity and integrating with global value chains, not by isolating India, and rests on five pillars (see diagram). It continues a long tradition of State-led development, now with a stronger role for private enterprise.

1. Key interventions

  • MSMEs: the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme kept small firms afloat, and the MSME definition was revised in 2020 to remove the fear of outgrowing benefits.
  • Manufacturing: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes for 14 sectors with an outlay of ₹1.97 lakh crore, and the Semicon India Programme (₹76,000 crore).
  • Defence: positive indigenisation lists and FDI up to 74% via the automatic route; defence production reached a record of about ₹1.78 lakh crore and exports ₹38,424 crore in 2025-26 (Ministry of Defence).
  • Agriculture: the ₹1 lakh crore Agriculture Infrastructure Fund for storage and post-harvest facilities.
  • Welfare: free foodgrains under the PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana (extended for five years from 2024) and One Nation One Ration Card for migrant workers.

2. Outcomes

  • Electronics: India became the world's second-largest mobile phone maker, with rising electronics exports.
  • Health security: indigenous COVID-19 vaccines supported domestic needs and Vaccine Maitri abroad.
  • Digital public infrastructure: UPI and other platforms show self-reliance in technology.
  • Semiconductors: assembly and fabrication units have been approved under the Semicon India Programme.

3. Concerns

  • Uneven gains: PLI benefits are concentrated in a few sectors, and disbursal has been slow.
  • Import dependence: electronic components, active pharmaceutical ingredients and solar equipment are still largely imported.
  • Protection risks: higher tariffs may breed inefficiency, and R&D spending stays below 1% of GDP.
  • Fiscal cost: incentives and credit guarantees strain public finances if they do not create scale.

4. Way forward

  • Deeper value chains: move from assembly to components, design and research.
  • Lower costs: PM GatiShakti (2021) and the National Logistics Policy (2022) aim to cut logistics costs and improve competitiveness.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh hosts one of the three Bulk Drug Parks approved in 2022 to cut import dependence for drug ingredients, and electronics clusters around Sri City and Tirupati benefit from PLI and Make in India.

Self-reliance must mean competitiveness with openness, built on research, skills and ease of doing business, as India moves towards Viksit Bharat @2047.
g1m-2023-p3-7b:
Civil service reformsMission KarmayogiCapacity buildingRule to role

Civil service reform means reshaping the recruitment, training, placement, performance and accountability of public servants so that a colonial, rule-bound and generalist bureaucracy becomes competent, citizen-centric and outcome-oriented. Many committees, from Kothari (1976) to the Second ARC (2008), have shaped this agenda, and Mission Karmayogi (2020) is its most recent large-scale step, focused on capacity building. The aim is a service that is professional, politically neutral and accountable for results.

1. Scope of reforms

  • Recruitment: age and attempt limits, aptitude and domain knowledge (Baswan Committee, 2016); lateral entry at Joint Secretary level since 2018 (an August 2024 advertisement was withdrawn over reservation concerns).
  • Training: induction, mid-career programmes and continuous learning, instead of one-time training at entry.
  • Placement and tenure: T.S.R. Subramanian v. Union of India (2013) directed minimum tenure and Civil Services Boards to curb arbitrary transfers.
  • Performance: online APAR (SPARROW), 360-degree appraisal for empanelment, and premature retirement of non-performers under FR 56(j).
  • Ethics and technology: a code of ethics and performance-linked career progression (Second ARC, 10th Report, 2008); e-Office, dashboards and data-driven decisions.

2. Mission Karmayogi

  • What it is: the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building, approved by the Union Cabinet in September 2020.
  • Aim: to make civil servants more creative, proactive, professional, transparent and technology-enabled.
  • Rule to role: it shifts training from "rule-based" to "role-based" using a Framework of Roles, Activities and Competencies.
  • Institutions: the Prime Minister's Public HR Council (apex), the Capacity Building Commission (2021) and Karmayogi Bharat, a non-profit SPV running the iGOT Karmayogi digital platform.
  • Coverage: about 46 lakh Central government employees, with annual capacity building plans for every ministry; States are also joining iGOT.

3. Challenges

  • Learning versus incentives: online courses help only if postings and promotions reward competence.
  • Reach: State and frontline staff need the same training, in local languages.
  • Measuring impact: course completions are easy to count, but changes in service delivery are harder to measure.
  • Resistance: generalist-specialist tensions and doubts about lateral entry slow wider reform.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats (2019) created over a lakh frontline posts; such grassroots staff need exactly the role-based, competency-driven training Karmayogi offers.

Capacity building must go hand in hand with stable tenure, accountability and political neutrality to give India a truly citizen-first civil service.
g1m-2023-p3-8a:
RTI Act 2005MKSSCivil societyRight to know

The Right to Information Act, 2005 (fully in force from 12 October 2005) replaced the Freedom of Information Act, 2002, which was never notified. The courts had earlier read the right to know into Article 19(1)(a) (Raj Narain, 1975; S.P. Gupta, 1981), but turning that principle into an enforceable law owed most to a grassroots civil society movement that began in the villages of Rajasthan.

1. Role of civil society

  • MKSS (1990, Rajasthan): the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan used jan sunwais (public hearings) on muster rolls and bills to expose fraud in relief works, with the slogan "our money, our accounts".
  • From village to nation: its 40-day dharna at Beawar (1996) made the right to information a national demand.
  • Drafting: the National Campaign for People's Right to Information (1996) and the Press Council of India drafted model bills.
  • State laws first: sustained pressure through public hearings, media and petitions produced laws in Tamil Nadu and Goa (1997), Rajasthan and Karnataka (2000), Delhi (2001) and Maharashtra (2002).
  • Final push: in 2004 the National Advisory Council, with civil society members, recast the Bill into a stronger law.

2. Other factors

  • Judiciary: judicial recognition of the right to know gave the demand constitutional legitimacy.
  • Political will: commitment by the government in 2004 and parliamentary scrutiny of the Bill.
  • Global trends: freedom-of-information laws worldwide, from Sweden's 1766 law onwards, offered models.

3. Assessment

  • Why it is largely true: the demand, the vocabulary ("our money, our accounts"), the model drafts and the sustained pressure all came from people's movements.
  • Why not wholly: the movement succeeded because it converged with judicial recognition and political will; civil society was the catalyst, not the only cause.

4. Present concerns

  • Autonomy: the 2019 amendment gave the Union power over Information Commissioners' tenure and salaries.
  • Exemptions: the DPDP Act, 2023 widened the personal-information exemption.
  • Implementation: vacancies in commissions and attacks on RTI users persist.
  • Achievements despite this: RTI has exposed irregularities in ration distribution, pensions and public works, and empowered ordinary citizens to question officials.

AP angle: the MKSS model of public hearings shaped Andhra Pradesh's pioneering social audits of the rural employment guarantee scheme from 2006, which use RTI-style disclosure of records.

Filling vacancies, protecting users and proactive disclosure under Section 4 will keep the Act true to its origins as a people's law.
g1m-2023-p3-8b:
NGOsThird sectorHuman rights advocacyFCRA

Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are voluntary, non-profit bodies independent of government, registered as societies (Societies Registration Act, 1860), trusts or Section 8 companies (Companies Act, 2013). Rooted in the freedom of association (Article 19(1)(c)), they form the "third sector" between the State and the market. In India they act as watchdogs, voices of the voiceless and partners in development, which is why they are central to building a more just and equitable society.

1. Promoting human rights

  • Litigation and advocacy: PUCL won the right-to-food orders (2001), Bandhua Mukti Morcha fought bonded labour, and Bachpan Bachao Andolan campaigned against child labour.
  • Monitoring abuses: NGOs document custodial violence, trafficking and discrimination, and support victims in courts and before human rights commissions.

2. Defending the marginalised

  • Informal workers: SEWA (1972) organised self-employed women workers into a trade union and cooperatives.
  • Forest dwellers: tribal and forest-dwellers' rights groups helped bring the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Women and children: shelters, legal aid and rescue of trafficked persons fill gaps in State services.

3. Creating a more just and equitable society

  • Just laws: MKSS's campaigns led to the RTI Act, 2005 and influenced MGNREGA.
  • Electoral accountability: the Association for Democratic Reforms won disclosure of candidates' criminal and financial records (2002) and was a petitioner in the electoral bonds case (2024).
  • Service delivery: Pratham's ASER surveys on learning levels, Akshaya Patra's mid-day meals, and health and disaster relief reach where the State is thin.
  • Evidence for policy: independent surveys and social audits give government feedback it cannot generate itself.

4. Concerns and regulation

  • Accountability gaps: weak transparency, donor dependence and misuse of foreign funds by some organisations damage the sector's credibility.
  • FCRA, 2010 (amended 2020): bars sub-granting of foreign funds, caps administrative expenses at 20% and requires an FCRA account at SBI, New Delhi; many licences have been cancelled, and critics see a chilling effect on advocacy groups.
  • Partnership tools: NITI Aayog's NGO Darpan portal and the National Policy on the Voluntary Sector (2007) aim at a trust-based relationship.

AP angle: the Rural Development Trust (since 1969) in drought-prone Anantapur works on education, health and the rights of Dalits, tribal communities and women, while NGOs have partnered Andhra Pradesh's self-help group movement.

With transparent funding and fair regulation that does not stifle dissent, NGOs remain indispensable partners in building a just and equitable society.
g1m-2023-p3-9a:
Article 323AAdministrative tribunalsL. Chandra KumarJudicial review

Article 323A, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), lets Parliament set up tribunals for disputes on recruitment and service conditions of public servants. The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 created the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) and allowed States to set up State Administrative Tribunals. The aim was to relieve High Courts of service cases and offer speedy, specialised justice. These bodies are quasi-judicial: they decide like courts but stand outside the regular judicial hierarchy.

1. Quasi-judicial nature

  • Adjudication: they decide service disputes between government and employees on evidence and law, and their orders bind the parties like decrees of a court.
  • Flexible procedure: they are not bound by the Code of Civil Procedure; they follow the principles of natural justice and regulate their own procedure.
  • Court-like powers: they have the powers of a civil court for summoning witnesses, requiring documents and reviewing decisions, and can punish for contempt.
  • Mixed benches: judicial and administrative members sit together, combining legal skill with administrative experience.

2. Are writs and appeals available?

  • Original scheme: Article 323A(2)(d) and Section 28 of the Act excluded the jurisdiction of all courts except the Supreme Court under Article 136; S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987) accepted this, treating tribunals as substitutes for High Courts.
  • L. Chandra Kumar (1997): a seven-judge bench struck down that exclusion, holding judicial review under Articles 226, 227 and 32 part of the basic structure.
  • Present route: a tribunal's order is challenged first before a Division Bench of the High Court in whose jurisdiction the tribunal lies, and then before the Supreme Court under Article 136; no direct appeal to the Supreme Court lies.
  • Limit: tribunals may examine the validity of laws, but cannot decide the validity of their own parent Act.

3. Recent developments

  • Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021: abolished several appellate tribunals and set uniform terms of service.
  • Madras Bar Association (19 November 2025): the Supreme Court struck down key appointment and tenure provisions of the 2021 Act as violating judicial independence and directed a National Tribunals Commission within four months.

AP angle: Article 371D (32nd Amendment, 1973) enabled the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal (set up 1975), a forerunner of Article 323A; P. Sambamurthy (1987) struck down the proviso letting the State government modify its orders. In 2019 the State government moved a proposal to close the tribunal.

Independent tribunals under High Court oversight can deliver both speed and the rule of law; a National Tribunals Commission would strengthen their independence.
g1m-2023-p3-9b:
IntegrityCorruptionProbityAnti-corruption institutions

Integrity in the civil services means consistency between public values and personal conduct: honesty, impartiality and incorruptibility, as reflected in the Nolan Committee's (UK, 1995) seven principles of public life. Its decline shows up as corruption, nepotism, collusion with vested interests and indifference to citizens, and it erodes public trust, efficiency and the rule of law. Both the causes and the remedies are partly individual and partly institutional.

1. Reasons for the decline of integrity

  • Politicisation: transfers and postings used as reward or punishment encourage collusion; T.S.R. Subramanian (2013) sought fixed tenure and Civil Services Boards.
  • Discretion without accountability: Klitgaard's formula, corruption = monopoly + discretion - accountability, explains rent-seeking in licensing, procurement and land records.
  • Complex rules and delays: cumbersome procedures and face-to-face dealings create opportunities for "speed money", especially in revenue, police, registration and municipal services.
  • Weak deterrence: slow investigation, delays in sanction for prosecution and low conviction rates reduce fear of punishment.
  • Social environment and weak ethics: social tolerance of corruption, consumerism and costly elections create demand for illicit money, while limited ethics training, few role models and poor protection for whistle-blowers leave honest officers isolated.

2. Institutional mechanism: laws

  • Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988: the 2018 amendment made bribe-giving an offence and added Section 17A, requiring prior approval to investigate decisions taken in official duty.
  • Supporting laws: PMLA 2002, the Benami Transactions Act (amended 2016), the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013, the Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014 and the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018.
  • Conduct rules: CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964 and AIS (Conduct) Rules, 1968, with annual declarations of assets.

3. Institutional mechanism: bodies and systems

  • Oversight: Vineet Narain (1997) led to statutory status for the CVC and its supervision of the CBI; Public Accounts Committees examine CAG reports.
  • Systemic tools: e-procurement, Direct Benefit Transfer, RTI, social audit and integrity pacts reduce discretion and face-to-face contact.
  • Gaps: delays in appointments and sanctions, overlapping agencies and low conviction rates limit the impact of this framework.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh has an Anti-Corruption Bureau with a toll-free complaint helpline, a Lokayukta under the AP Lokayukta and Upa-Lokayukta Act, 1983, and a Vigilance and Enforcement Department.

Laws and agencies deter, but lasting integrity also needs value-based training, secure tenure, simple procedures and leaders who set an example.
g1m-2023-p3-10a:
Citizen's CharterSevottamRight to ServicesCitizen-centric administration

A Citizen's Charter is a public declaration by a service-providing organisation of its services, standards, timelines, grievance redress and citizens' obligations. It began in the UK in 1991 under John Major. India adopted it after the Conference of Chief Ministers (1997) on effective and responsive government, with the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) as the nodal agency. Its record in India has been mixed.

1. The Indian experience

  • Spread: charters were drafted by central ministries, States and public bodies such as banks, hospitals, railways and municipal corporations, and displayed at service counters and on websites.
  • Sevottam (DARPG, 2006): linked charters with grievance redress and service delivery capability; the BIS standard IS 15700:2005 set quality norms.
  • Second ARC, 12th Report (2009): "Citizen Centric Administration" asked for charters that are specific, consultative and backed by redress.
  • From charter to right: the Citizens' Right to Grievance Redress Bill, 2011 lapsed in 2014, but many States passed Right to Services Acts, starting with Madhya Pradesh (2010); CPGRAMS handles grievances online.

2. Shortcomings

  • Top-down drafting: charters were drafted without consulting users or front-line staff.
  • Vague promises: standards were unmeasurable and seldom updated.
  • No teeth: no legal enforceability or compensation for failure.
  • Low awareness: citizens did not know of charters, and staff were untrained and unmotivated.
  • One-time exercise: many charters copied a common format, ignored local conditions and did not change the work culture behind the counter.

3. Solutions to improve impact

  • Statutory backing: time-bound delivery with compensation and penalties, as in Right to Services laws.
  • Participatory drafting: measurable standards for each service, revised regularly with users, and a clear statement of what citizens must provide, so that both sides share responsibility.
  • Grievance redress: deadlines, escalation to higher officers and independent audit.
  • Awareness and technology: local-language publicity, integration with e-governance and real-time feedback.
  • Incentives: charter compliance linked to officials' performance appraisal, with recognition for offices that meet their standards.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats display service-wise timelines, and the Mana Mitra WhatsApp governance service (2025) delivers certificates and services online, turning charter promises into deliverables.

The charter idea in India has moved from voluntary declarations towards rights-based delivery. Charters work only when they become enforceable rights; legal backing, participation and monitoring can complete that shift.
g1m-2023-p3-10b:
Dimensions of governanceAdministrative governanceAccountabilityCitizen-centricity

Governance is "the manner in which power is exercised in the management of a country's economic and social resources for development" (World Bank, 1992). It is wider than government, as it includes the market and civil society. UNDP (1997) identified three core dimensions: economic, political and administrative. Good governance adds normative qualities such as participation, transparency, equity and the rule of law. Of these dimensions, the administrative dimension is the machinery through which policies are turned into services for citizens.

1. Dimensions of governance

  • Political: the process by which governments are chosen, held accountable and replaced; legitimacy, free elections and protection of rights.
  • Economic: decision-making that affects economic activity, such as fiscal management, growth policy and regulation of markets.
  • Administrative: the system of policy implementation through an efficient, independent and accountable public sector.
  • Social and legal: participation, inclusion and equity involving civil society, and access to justice with impartial enforcement of laws.
  • Newer dimensions: environmental governance of shared resources and digital governance of data and platforms.

2. The administrative dimension

It is the machinery of the State that turns policy into services, through an efficient, accountable and responsive public administration. It decides whether a good law or scheme actually reaches the last citizen, and it is what citizens experience in a ration shop, a police station or a revenue office.

3. Key components

  • Efficiency and effectiveness: outcome focus, timely delivery and performance measurement through dashboards and outcome budgets.
  • Accountability and transparency: RTI, CAG audits, social audits and the Lokpal make officials answerable for their decisions and spending.
  • Responsiveness: Citizen's Charters, grievance redress through CPGRAMS and Right to Services laws put the citizen at the centre.
  • Capacity and integrity: merit-based recruitment, capacity building through Mission Karmayogi, and conduct rules and vigilance that keep discretion in check.
  • Decentralisation and technology: functions, funds and functionaries devolved under the 73rd and 74th Amendments; DigiLocker, Direct Benefit Transfer and e-Office cut delays and leakages, while PM GatiShakti breaks departmental silos.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats (2019) bring administration to the doorstep, its Real Time Governance Society uses integrated data for monitoring, and the Mana Mitra WhatsApp service (2025) offers services online.

Administrative governance that is simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent (SMART) is the foundation of good governance, because it is where citizens actually meet the State.
g1m-2023-p3-11a:
Ethics in public serviceConstitutional moralityNaitik BharatParliamentary democracy

Parliamentary democracy rests on a chain of trust: the executive is accountable to the legislature, and legislators to the people. Ethics in public service, meaning integrity, impartiality, accountability and compassion, keeps this chain intact, because laws and institutions are only as good as the people who run them. "Naitik Bharat" is the idea of an ethical India, where public conduct follows constitutional morality and citizens, officials and leaders share a common code of values.

1. Why ethics is essential to parliamentary democracy

  • Legitimacy: citizens obey laws they see as fairly made and fairly applied; unethical conduct erodes consent.
  • Delivery: honest administration ensures that welfare reaches the last person, as Gandhi's talisman asks.
  • Constitutional morality: Ambedkar warned that a Constitution, however good, works only as well as those who run it.
  • Accountability chain: ministerial responsibility works only if ministers and officials tell Parliament the truth and accept responsibility for failures.

2. Present challenges

  • Criminalisation: 46% of Lok Sabha members elected in 2024 declared criminal cases (ADR).
  • Money power and defections: costly elections and opaque funding weaken the link between representatives and voters.
  • Institutional strain: corruption, frequent disruptions of legislatures and misinformation lower public trust.
  • Conflict of interest: links between business and politics, and post-retirement appointments, blur the line between public duty and private gain.

3. Pathway towards Naitik Bharat

  • Codes: codes of ethics and conduct for ministers, legislators and civil servants (Second ARC, 4th Report, "Ethics in Governance", 2007) and stronger Ethics Committees of Parliament.
  • Institutions: an effective Lokpal, Lokayuktas and CVC, and operationalising the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.
  • Electoral reform: decriminalisation (Public Interest Foundation, 2018), transparent party funding after the electoral bonds verdict (2024) and inner-party democracy.
  • Civil services and technology: ethics modules under Mission Karmayogi and value-based appraisal; DBT, e-procurement and faceless processes cut discretion.
  • Society: value education (NEP 2020 stresses ethical and constitutional values), Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) and ethical role models in public life.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh created a post of Advisor on Students' Ethics and Values in 2024 to strengthen moral education in schools; Telugu moral traditions such as Vemana's verses offer rich material for this.

Naitik Bharat will come not from laws alone but from ethics becoming a habit of leaders, officials and citizens alike. When rules, institutions and personal conscience pull in the same direction, democracy earns trust, in the spirit of Satyameva Jayate.
g1m-2023-p3-11b:
AccountabilityAnswerabilityEnforceabilityCivil service reforms

Accountability is the obligation of a public official to answer for decisions and results to a higher authority, the legislature, the courts and citizens, and to face consequences for failure. It has two elements: answerability (explaining and justifying actions) and enforceability (rewards and sanctions). In a democracy, civil servants are accountable to ministers, and through them to Parliament, as well as directly to the law and to citizens.

1. Meaning and forms

  • Answerability: the duty to explain and justify decisions, through reports, audits, questions in the legislature and RTI replies.
  • Enforceability: the possibility of rewards and sanctions, from promotions to disciplinary action and prosecution.
  • Multiple directions: accountability runs upward to superiors, outward to citizens and inward to professional ethics (see diagram).

2. Factors that have weakened accountability

  • Legal protection: Article 311 guards against arbitrary dismissal, and prior sanction for prosecution (Section 218 BNSS, formerly Section 197 CrPC; Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act) is often delayed.
  • Anonymity: under ministerial responsibility civil servants are not publicly answerable, and collective file-based decisions diffuse responsibility.
  • Process over outcomes: a colonial, rule-bound culture values procedure over results, and vague targets and inflated, subjective appraisals mean that performance rarely affects careers.
  • Political interference: frequent transfers weaken ownership of results and encourage loyalty to patrons rather than to the public.
  • Weak enforcement: slow disciplinary proceedings, information asymmetry, weak citizen participation and poor protection for whistle-blowers mean that failures rarely carry consequences.

3. Ways to improve accountability mechanisms

  • Performance: outcome budgets and measurable key performance indicators for each office; revive performance agreements like the Results-Framework Documents (2009), which linked ministries' targets to annual evaluation.
  • Appraisal: 360-degree appraisal, premature retirement of non-performers under FR 56(j) and performance-linked promotions (Second ARC).
  • Citizens: proactive disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act, social audits, Citizen's Charters with compensation and Right to Services laws.
  • Oversight: Lokpal, CVC, CAG performance audits and parliamentary committees such as the Public Accounts Committee.
  • Technology and fairness: e-Office, real-time dashboards and online grievance tracking (CPGRAMS); clear delegation and time-bound sanction decisions protect honest officers, so that accountability does not breed fear of decision-making.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency (2009), one of India's first independent social audit units, takes rural employment scheme records to Gram Sabhas, making officials answerable to the people they serve.

Accountability should be for outcomes, not merely for following procedure. Balancing answerability with protection of bona fide decisions and citizen oversight can create a civil service that is both fearless and responsive to the people it serves.
g1m-2023-p3-12a:
ValuesPersonalitySocio-cultural systemsPurusharthas

Values are enduring beliefs about what is desirable that guide choices and conduct. Milton Rokeach (1973) divided them into terminal values (end goals such as freedom or wisdom) and instrumental values (modes of conduct such as honesty or courage). Family, education, religion, peers, media and society shape them. Values are the bridge between the individual and society: they mould personality and, when shared, sustain the norms and institutions of a culture.

1. Significance in the development of personality

  • Core of character: values shape goals, decisions and moral judgement, giving integrity and consistency to behaviour.
  • Motivation and self-concept: they give meaning, direction and resilience in hardship.
  • Moral growth: they guide the movement from self-interest to principled reasoning, as in Kohlberg's stages of moral development.
  • Emotional balance: values such as patience, tolerance and self-control help a person manage emotions and resolve conflicts.
  • Relationships and leadership: empathy and fairness build trust; Gandhi's truth and non-violence shaped his whole personality and his leadership.

2. Significance in socio-cultural systems

  • Basis of order: values underlie norms, customs, institutions and laws, and shared values bind society (Durkheim's collective conscience).
  • Identity and continuity: they carry cultural identity across generations through festivals, literature, art and family traditions, giving people a sense of belonging.
  • Engine of reform: equality and dignity drove social reform and the abolition of untouchability (Article 17).
  • Constitutional values: the Preamble itself is a value statement of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

3. Hierarchy of values in India

  • Traditional order: dharma regulates artha and kama, and moksha is the highest goal; duties come before rights, and the family and community before the individual.
  • Life stages: the four ashramas (brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha, sannyasa) arranged these goals across a lifetime, moving from learning and worldly duties to detachment.
  • Gandhian synthesis: Gandhi placed truth and non-violence at the top and insisted that pure ends need pure means.
  • Present-day shift: constitutional morality (dignity, equality, secularism) now ranks highest in public life, while markets push individualism, creating value conflicts.

AP angle: Telugu literature has carried values to the masses: Vemana's and the Sumati Satakam's verses teach honesty and humility, and Gurajada Apparao wrote that a nation is not its soil but its people.

Harmonising traditional and constitutional values through family, schools and media builds balanced individuals and a cohesive, humane society.
g1m-2023-p3-12b:
Vinoba BhaveBhoodanSarvodayaGram Swaraj

Acharya Vinoba Bhave (1895-1982), Gandhi's spiritual heir and the first individual satyagrahi (1940), began the Bhoodan movement at Pochampalli (Nalgonda district, now in Telangana) on 18 April 1951, when V. Ramachandra Reddy donated 100 acres to landless Dalits. Through moral persuasion rather than law or force, he sought Sarvodaya, the welfare of all. He received the first Ramon Magsaysay Award for community leadership (1958) and the Bharat Ratna posthumously (1983).

1. His reform ideology

  • Sarvodaya: welfare of all through a non-violent change of heart rather than coercion or class struggle.
  • Gift movements: Bhoodan (gift of land), then Gramdan (village ownership of land), Sampattidan (gift of wealth) and Shramdan (gift of labour).
  • Gram Swaraj: self-reliant, self-governing villages as the base of democracy.
  • Lok Niti over Raj Niti: the moral power of the people rather than the power of the State.
  • Personal ethics: simplicity, non-possession, service and "Jai Jagat" (victory to the world).

2. How it nurtured an ethical atmosphere in public life

  • Leadership as service: walking across India for years, he showed that leadership means persuasion and service, not power.
  • Moral force in conflict: his peace mission saw Chambal dacoits surrender (1960), showing the power of trust and dialogue.
  • Voluntary giving: over 40 lakh acres were pledged, creating a climate of sharing in a deeply unequal society.
  • Inspiring others: leaders such as Jayaprakash Narayan left party politics to dedicate their lives (jeevandan) to the Sarvodaya movement.

3. Relevance in modern times

  • Inequality: persisting landlessness calls for land reforms and the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
  • Decentralisation: Gram Swaraj anticipates the 73rd Amendment and empowered Gram Sabhas.
  • Trusteeship and giving: CSR under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013 and philanthropy echo Sampattidan.
  • Conflict and sustainability: dialogue and land justice in Left-Wing Extremism areas; non-possession matches Mission LiFE's sustainable living.
  • Public ethics: selfless service is an antidote to money power and corruption.

4. Limits

  • Implementation gaps: much of the pledged land was uncultivable or never distributed.
  • Voluntarism alone is not enough: moral appeal cannot replace legal reform and strong institutions.

AP angle: Bhoodan was born in the Telugu region amid agrarian unrest, and the Andhra Pradesh Bhoodan and Gramdan Act, 1965 was enacted to govern the donated lands.

Vinoba's moral persuasion and selfless service, backed by strong institutions, remain a guide for ethical public life today.
g1m-2023-p3-13a:
AttitudeTheory of Planned BehaviourCognitive dissonancePolitical polarisation

An attitude is a learned tendency to evaluate a person, object or idea favourably or unfavourably. It has three components (ABC model): affective (feelings), behavioural (tendency to act) and cognitive (beliefs). Attitudes influence behaviour, but the link is neither automatic nor one-way. In politics, strongly held attitudes can harden into polarisation, which is increasingly visible in India.

1. Do attitudes influence behaviour?

  • Yes, often: in Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behaviour, attitudes, social norms and perceived control shape intentions that drive behaviour; strong, specific attitudes formed by personal experience predict behaviour best.
  • Not always: in LaPiere's study (1934), hotels that had served a Chinese couple later said in letters that they would refuse Chinese guests. Situational pressure, social norms and competing attitudes weaken the link.
  • Strength and specificity matter: a specific attitude (towards voting in this election) predicts behaviour better than a general one (towards politics), and attitudes that come to mind easily guide action more.
  • Two-way link: behaviour also shapes attitudes through cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957); laws against untouchability changed attitudes over time.

2. Polarisation of political attitudes in India

  • Meaning: growing distance and hostility between political camps, both ideological and affective (dislike of opponents' supporters).
  • Social drivers: identity politics of religion, caste, language and region turns political choice into a question of group loyalty.
  • Media drivers: social-media echo chambers, misinformation, algorithmic amplification, personality-centred campaigns and partisan media reward outrage over reasoned debate.
  • Manifestations: legislative disruptions, hate speech, online trolling and Centre-State friction along party lines.
  • Consequences: erosion of trust, consensus and social harmony, although political engagement and turnout remain high.

3. Way forward

  • Legal limits: enforce the Model Code of Conduct and Section 123 of the Representation of the People Act; in Abhiram Singh (2017) the Supreme Court held that seeking votes on religion, caste, race, community or language is a corrupt practice.
  • Informed citizens: media and digital literacy, fact-checking and deliberative forums.
  • Civic culture: constitutional values and respect for opponents taught in schools and practised by leaders.
  • Consensus forums: all-party meetings and parliamentary committees, where members often work across party lines, help build agreement.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's closely fought, largely two-way contests and intense social-media campaigns show how political loyalty can harden into social identity even in villages.

Promoting constitutional values, dialogue and tolerance of differing views can turn political competition into healthy democratic debate.
g1m-2023-p3-13b:
PersuasionElaboration Likelihood ModelBehaviour changeJan Bhagidari

Persuasion is the process of changing a person's attitudes or behaviour through communication, without coercion or deception. The Yale (Hovland) approach frames it as "who says what to whom, and how": the source, the message, the audience and the channel together decide whether a message changes minds. For civil servants, persuasion is a democratic tool to turn government programmes into people's movements (Jan Andolan), which is central to the idea of a "New India".

1. Constructs of persuasion

  • Source: credibility (expertise and trustworthiness), attractiveness and similarity to the audience; people trust a local ASHA worker more than a distant poster.
  • Message: rational or emotional appeal, one-sided or two-sided arguments, framing (gain or loss) and repetition.
  • Audience and channel: prior attitudes, involvement, education and mood decide how a message is received, through face-to-face talk, mass media or social media.
  • Routes (Elaboration Likelihood Model, Petty and Cacioppo): highly involved audiences take the central route and are moved by strong arguments, with lasting change; others take the peripheral route, swayed by cues such as authority or celebrity, with short-lived change.
  • Psychological principles: Cialdini's six principles, namely reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity.

2. Can civil servants use persuasion for a "New India"? Yes

  • Behaviour change goals: many goals depend on behaviour, not just funds; the Swachh Bharat Mission used community-led sanitation and swachhagrahis, and rural India was declared open-defecation free on 2 October 2019.
  • Voluntary sacrifice: under "Give It Up", over one crore consumers voluntarily surrendered their LPG subsidy.
  • Public health and gender: Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, COVID-19 vaccination and nudges (Economic Survey 2018-19) show the power of persuasion.
  • Ownership: persuasion respects autonomy and builds lasting ownership, unlike coercion, which breeds resentment and evasion.
  • Credible, two-way communication: ASHAs, teachers and self-help group leaders make messages trusted and local, and platforms such as MyGov let citizens give ideas and feedback, turning publicity into dialogue.

3. Limits

  • Ethical boundaries: persuasion must be truthful and transparent, never manipulation or propaganda.
  • Respect for dissent: it must allow disagreement and complement, not replace, the rule of law and good service delivery.
  • Credibility is earned: messages fail when services are poor; persuasion works only when the State delivers on its promises.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming (since 2016, run by Rythu Sadhikara Samstha) spread largely through farmer-to-farmer persuasion by community resource persons and field demonstrations.

Ethical persuasion that informs rather than manipulates, and turns schemes into people's movements, is a key democratic tool for building Viksit Bharat.
g1m-2023-p3-14a:
Popular democracyPublic trustEthical leadershipNolan principles

Popular democracy rests on mass participation and the people's mandate. When it turns populist, with short-term promises, personality cults and emotive mobilisation, a gap opens between promise and performance, and this can breed distrust of representatives, though not necessarily of democracy itself. Ethical leadership, which puts public interest above personal or party gain, is the bridge that can restore trust between the people and those they elect.

1. Why distrust arises

  • Unfulfilled promises: competitive freebies and grand announcements that strain finances raise expectations that cannot be met.
  • Distance from voters: weak constituency work and decisions driven by party high commands make citizens feel unheard between elections.
  • Criminalisation: 46% of Lok Sabha members elected in 2024 declared criminal cases (ADR).
  • Money power: costly elections and opaque funding; the Supreme Court struck down electoral bonds in 2024.
  • Defections and disruptions: defections despite the Tenth Schedule (1985), "resort politics", disrupted legislatures, fewer sittings and polarising rhetoric amplified by social media.

2. Why distrust is not the whole story

  • High participation: Lok Sabha 2024 turnout was about 65.8%, with women voting on par with men.
  • Accountability works: peaceful transfers of power, a free media, RTI and courts keep representatives answerable.
  • Faith in the ballot: frequent anti-incumbency verdicts show that voters punish poor performance through elections rather than rejecting democracy.

3. Scope of ethical leadership in democracy and politics

  • Values: the Nolan principles (see diagram), plus empathy; Gandhi stressed that pure ends need pure means.
  • Leading by example: Lal Bahadur Shastri resigned as Railway Minister in 1956 after a rail accident, owning moral responsibility.
  • Institutional support: codes of conduct for legislators, effective Ethics Committees, inner-party democracy, decriminalisation and State funding of elections (Indrajit Gupta Committee, 1998).
  • Servant leadership: listening, consensus-building and respect for opponents turn competition into cooperation for the public good.
  • Long-term vision: ethical leaders explain hard choices honestly rather than promising what cannot be delivered, and protect institutions even when it costs them politically.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh recorded turnout above 80% in the 2024 simultaneous elections, showing deep public faith in the vote; Tanguturi Prakasam, "Andhra Kesari" and first Chief Minister of Andhra State (1953), is remembered for courage and simplicity in public life.

Distrust of representatives is a warning, not a verdict against democracy. Ethical leadership converts electoral mandates into public trust, the real foundation of a mature democracy.
g1m-2023-p3-14b:
International ethicsPeaceful settlementClimate justiceGlobal commons

International ethics is the set of moral principles that guide relations among States and peoples: sovereignty, non-intervention, justice, human rights, peace and care for the global commons. It tempers pure realism (power and national interest) with idealist and cosmopolitan ideas of a shared humanity. India's approach draws on Panchsheel (1954) and Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam ("the world is one family"). Ethics matters most where power alone cannot deliver order: in settling disputes and in protecting the environment.

1. Significance in international dispute resolution

  • Charter principles: the UN Charter requires peaceful settlement of disputes (Article 2(3)) and bars the threat or use of force (Article 2(4)); Article 33 lists negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration and judicial settlement.
  • Good faith: ethics demands that treaties be honoured (pacta sunt servanda), that States show restraint and accept awards. India accepted the 2014 arbitral award on its maritime boundary with Bangladesh and implemented the Land Boundary Agreement in 2015 (100th Amendment).
  • Humanity in war: humanitarian law (Geneva Conventions) protects civilians, the wounded and prisoners even in armed conflict.
  • Rule over might: rule-based settlement replaces "might is right" and protects smaller States.

2. Significance in environmental cooperation

  • Global commons: the atmosphere, oceans and biodiversity belong to all; without ethics comes the "tragedy of the commons".
  • Climate justice: common but differentiated responsibilities (Rio, 1992), since developed countries caused most historical emissions.
  • Cooperation that works: the Montreal Protocol (1987) on the ozone layer, the Paris Agreement (2015) and COP29's (2024) climate finance goal of at least $300 billion a year by 2035.
  • India's role: the International Solar Alliance (2015), Mission LiFE (2022), the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (2019) and a net-zero target for 2070.

3. Challenges

  • Power politics: use of the veto in the Security Council, unilateral sanctions and non-compliance with international rulings show the limits of ethics without enforcement.
  • Trust deficit: delays in meeting the promise of $100 billion a year in climate finance by 2020 weakened developing countries' trust.
  • Free-riding: every country gains from a stable climate, but each is tempted to let others bear the cost.

AP angle: cyclones such as Michaung (2023) and Montha (2025) make global climate cooperation and adaptation finance vital for Andhra Pradesh; at home, its river disputes go to the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal, a domestic model of peaceful settlement.

An international order based on justice, dialogue and shared responsibility is the path to lasting peace and a liveable planet.
g1m-2023-p3-15a:
Substantive lawProcedural lawUbi jus ibi remediumDue process

Law is broadly divided into substantive law, which defines rights, duties, liabilities, offences and punishments, and procedural (adjective) law, which lays down the machinery for enforcing them in courts. The first says what the law is; the second says how it is applied. The two are distinct in nature and purpose, yet they depend on each other: a right is meaningful only when there is a fair procedure to enforce it.

1. Differences

  • Nature: substantive law creates and defines rights and duties; procedural law provides the steps for filing, investigation, trial, evidence and appeal.
  • Examples: substantive, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (replacing the IPC) and the Indian Contract Act, 1872; procedural, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (replacing the CrPC) and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Evidence law (Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023) is adjective law. The new criminal laws took effect on 1 July 2024.
  • Retrospectivity: penal laws cannot punish past acts (Article 20(1)); procedural changes usually apply to pending cases, as no one has a vested right in procedure.
  • Effect: substantive law decides the outcome of a case; procedural law governs how that outcome is reached.
  • Interpretation: penal provisions are construed strictly, while procedural rules are construed liberally so that technicalities do not defeat justice.

2. Interrelationship

  • Complementary: a right without a remedy is meaningless (ubi jus ibi remedium), and procedure without substantive rights has no purpose.
  • Procedure serves justice: in State of Punjab v. Shamlal Murari (1976), the Supreme Court said processual law "is not to be a tyrant but a servant, not an obstruction but an aid to justice".
  • Fair procedure as a right: in Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Court held that procedure under Article 21 must itself be just, fair and reasonable.
  • Combined statutes: laws like the POCSO Act, 2012 contain both offences and child-friendly trial procedures.

3. Why both matter for justice delivery

  • Overlap: a procedural rule can decide substantive rights; under Section 27 of the Limitation Act, 1963, failure to sue for possession in time extinguishes the right to the property itself.
  • Delay defeats rights: when procedure is slow, substantive rights exist only on paper; justice delayed is justice denied.
  • Procedural reform: the new criminal laws introduce timelines, electronic summons and videography of searches and seizures to make trials faster and fairer.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's Disha Bill, 2019 combined substantive change (harsher punishment for crimes against women) with procedural change (investigation in 7 and trial in 14 working days); it has not received Presidential assent.

Justice requires both: clear substantive rights and simple, fair and speedy procedures to enforce them.
g1m-2023-p3-15b:
Direct taxesImpact and incidenceTax reformsIncome-tax Act 2025

A direct tax is levied on a person's income or wealth, and its impact (initial burden) and incidence (final burden) fall on the same person. Personal income tax and corporation tax are the main examples (Union taxes under Entries 82 and 85 of List I). Indirect taxes such as GST, by contrast, are collected from sellers but shifted forward to consumers. Direct taxes are therefore generally non-transferable and progressive.

1. Transferable or non-transferable?

  • Generally non-transferable: an income-tax payer cannot shift the burden to anyone else, which makes direct taxes progressive and equitable.
  • Partial shifting in practice: economists note that corporation tax may be partly shifted through higher prices, lower wages or lower dividends.
  • Contrast with indirect taxes: GST is paid by the seller to the government but borne by the final consumer.

2. Recent direct tax reforms

  • Corporate tax cut (2019): 22% for domestic companies forgoing exemptions and 15% for new manufacturing firms, to boost investment.
  • New personal tax regime (2020): lower rates without exemptions, the default from 2023-24; Budget 2025-26 made income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free under it (₹12.75 lakh for salaried taxpayers).
  • Simplification: the Dividend Distribution Tax was abolished (2020), and capital gains were rationalised in 2024 (long-term gains taxed at 12.5%, short-term gains on listed equity at 20%).
  • Trust-based administration: faceless assessment and appeals and a Taxpayers' Charter (2020); the retrospective tax on indirect transfers was scrapped (2021), and Vivad se Vishwas schemes (2020, 2024) settled disputes.
  • New law: the Income-tax Act, 2025, in force from 1 April 2026, replaced the 1961 Act with simpler language and a single "tax year"; Budget 2026-27 kept slabs unchanged, cut TCS on overseas tour packages and on education and medical remittances to 2%, and decriminalised minor offences.

3. Significance and concerns

  • Equity and buoyancy: progressive direct taxes reduce inequality and grow with incomes, giving stable revenue.
  • Narrow base: a small share of people pay income tax, and agricultural income is outside the Union's reach (taxes on agricultural income are a State subject, Entry 46, List II).

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh receives about 4.2% of the divisible pool of Union taxes under the 16th Finance Commission (2026-31), so buoyant direct tax collections strengthen its finances.

Simple rates, a wider base and trust-based administration can make direct taxes the backbone of a fair and growth-friendly tax system.
g1m-2023-p4-2a:
Monetary policy transmissionRepo rateExternal benchmarkLiquidity

Monetary policy transmission is the pass-through of a change in the RBI's policy repo rate, set by the six-member Monetary Policy Committee (Sec. 45ZB, RBI Act), to money-market rates, bank deposit and lending rates, bond yields and the exchange rate, and then to spending, output and inflation. Its speed and completeness decide how effective inflation targeting can be.

1. Channels of transmission

  • Interest-rate channel: cheaper or costlier loans change household and business spending on homes, vehicles and machinery.
  • Credit channel: banks' ability and willingness to lend change with their funding costs and balance sheets.
  • Exchange-rate and asset-price channels: rate changes move capital flows, the rupee, bond and share prices, and hence wealth and imports.
  • Expectations channel: credible forward guidance anchors inflation expectations, wage demands and price setting.

2. Issues in transmission

  • Internal benchmarks: the Base Rate (2010) and MCLR (2016) followed banks' own cost of funds, so they moved slowly and passed on hikes faster than cuts.
  • Deposit rigidity: most deposits are fixed-rate, and administered small-savings rates compete with banks, so deposit rates, and hence lending rates, fall slowly.
  • Fiscal dominance: heavy government borrowing keeps G-sec yields high and blunts rate cuts.
  • Liquidity and balance sheets: liquidity deficits block the pass-through of cuts, and high NPAs (2015-19) made banks risk-averse.
  • Structural limits: informal credit, a low credit-GDP ratio and supply-driven food inflation lie beyond the reach of interest rates.

In the 2025 easing (repo cut by 125 bps to 5.25%), externally benchmarked loans repriced quickly, while MCLR loans and deposit rates lagged.

3. Steps to overcome these issues

  • Wider external benchmarks: extend the External Benchmark Lending Rate, mandatory for new floating-rate retail and MSME loans since 1 October 2019 and reset at least once in three months, to more segments.
  • Active liquidity management: the Standing Deposit Facility floor (2022), variable-rate repo and reverse repo auctions, and the CRR cut to 3% (2025) keep the overnight rate close to the repo rate.
  • Small savings: link their rates strictly to G-sec yields under the Shyamala Gopinath Committee formula.
  • Fiscal and market reforms: lower deficits, deeper bond markets, floating-rate deposits and clear forward guidance.

AP angle: 93.2% of Andhra Pradesh's farm households are indebted (NSS 77th round, 2019), many to informal lenders whom policy rates never reach; financial inclusion through banks, SHGs and Stree Nidhi itself improves transmission.

Faster, symmetric transmission makes inflation targeting credible at a lower cost to growth.
g1m-2023-p4-2b:
Fiscal policy toolsCustoms dutyCentral exciseInflation control

Fiscal policy is the use of government revenue, spending and borrowing, presented through the Annual Financial Statement (Article 112; Article 202 for States), to perform Musgrave's functions of allocation, redistribution and stabilisation. Within the limits of the FRBM Act, 2003, its tools can raise revenue or cool prices, and indirect taxes such as customs and excise are among the quickest to change.

1. Fiscal policy tools in India

  • Taxation: direct taxes (income and corporation tax) and indirect taxes (GST, customs, excise), plus cesses and surcharges, decide both revenue and incentives.
  • Public expenditure: revenue spending (salaries, subsidies, DBT) supports demand, while capital spending (₹12.2 lakh crore in 2026-27) builds future capacity.
  • Borrowing and debt management: dated securities, treasury bills and small savings finance the deficit within FRBM targets; automatic monetisation through ad hoc treasury bills ended in 1997.
  • Subsidies and transfers: food and fertiliser subsidies, MSP, tax incentives (PLI, SEZ) and Finance Commission transfers.

2. Customs and excise as flexible tools: the case for

  • Quick changes by notification: the Customs Act 1962 (Sec. 25 exemptions) and the Customs Tariff Act 1975 (Sec. 8A emergency increases, safeguard and anti-dumping duties) let the government act between Budgets.
  • Inflation control: excise on petrol and diesel was cut in November 2021 and May 2022; edible-oil import duties were cut (crude oils to 10% in 2025); export duties on rice and onions (2023) cooled domestic prices.
  • Revenue: fuel excise was raised when crude prices crashed in 2020; a windfall tax on domestic crude ran from July 2022 to December 2024; excise on tobacco replaced the GST compensation cess in 2026.

3. Limits

  • Narrow base: after GST, central excise covers only five petroleum products (crude, petrol, diesel, ATF, natural gas) and tobacco.
  • Conflicting aims: duty cuts to curb prices cost revenue, so the two goals pull in opposite directions.
  • External constraints: WTO bound rates and FTAs limit customs changes; frequent changes hurt predictability and create inverted duty structures.
  • Federal cost: cesses and surcharges lie outside the divisible pool (Art. 270), so States lose when the Centre relies on them.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh, India's largest oil-palm producer, sees farm-gate prices fall when edible-oil import duties are cut: consumer and farmer interests pull apart.

Customs and excise are useful short-term levers, but lasting price stability rests on monetary policy, supply management and a predictable tax regime.
g1m-2023-p4-3a:
Externally aided projectsAPIIATPClimate resilienceMinor-tank irrigation

Externally aided projects (EAPs) are development projects financed by loans or grants from multilateral (World Bank, ADB, AIIB, NDB, IFAD) or bilateral (JICA, KfW) agencies. Because a State cannot borrow abroad (Article 293), loans come through the Union's Department of Economic Affairs and are passed on back-to-back to general-category States, which bear the repayment. In AP, the APIIATP is a leading example.

1. Funding and objectives of APIIATP

  • Funding: the Andhra Pradesh Integrated Irrigation and Agriculture Transformation Project has a World Bank (IBRD) loan of US$172.2 million, approved in October 2018 with a 6-year grace period and 24-year maturity, plus the State's counterpart share; it was planned for 2018-25.
  • Objective: to raise the agricultural productivity, profitability and climate resilience of smallholders in 12 of AP's most climate-vulnerable, drought-prone districts.
  • Scale: about 1,000 small-scale community-based irrigation systems (minor tanks), covering roughly 90,000 ha in over 1,000 villages.
  • Activities: tank rehabilitation, drought-tolerant seeds, climate-smart practices and crop diversification, tank fisheries and livestock, weather-based advisories, and post-harvest and market links.

2. Principles

  • Climate resilience first: drought-proofing through tanks, better seeds and advisories is at the core of farm growth.
  • Convergence: the Water Resources, Agriculture, Horticulture, Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Ground Water departments work together in the same villages.
  • Community ownership: Water Users' Associations (WUAs) plan, maintain and manage the tanks.
  • Conjunctive use: surface water and groundwater are managed together to avoid over-extraction.
  • Markets and inclusion: Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) link farmers to markets, with priority for women and vulnerable groups.

3. Scope of beneficiaries

The project targets over 2 lakh farm families. It builds on the World Bank-aided community tank management project (2007-16), which rehabilitated 975 tanks in today's AP, and extends the tank-based approach from irrigation alone to the whole farm economy.

  • Wider gains: recharge of groundwater around tanks benefits nearby well owners, and drought-proofing reduces distress migration from dry districts.
  • Other AP examples of EAPs: the World Bank-aided AP Disaster Recovery Project after Cyclone Hudhud, and World Bank and ADB loans for the Amaravati capital (Union Budget 2024-25).

EAPs bring finance and design expertise; lasting gains depend on WUAs maintaining the tanks and on viable FPOs after the loan ends, so community ownership must be built in from the start.
g1m-2023-p4-3b:
AP Reorganisation Act 2014Resource gapSectoral shiftResource mobilisation

The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 divided the State on 2 June 2014. Residual Andhra Pradesh kept about 58% of the population (Census 2011) and a matching share of the debt, but lost Hyderabad, the hub of services, IT and own-tax revenue. The result was an economy tilted towards agriculture and a structural resource gap between revenue and commitments.

1. Sectoral changes

  • Agrarian tilt: agriculture and allied sectors form about one-third of AP's GSVA against about 18% nationally, as Hyderabad's IT, finance and corporate headquarters stayed in Telangana.
  • Thin services base: AP lost a mega-city's agglomeration economies; services now depend on smaller cities such as Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati.
  • Concentrated industry: manufacturing clusters in Visakhapatnam, Sri City and Krishnapatnam, and aquaculture-led growth in the deltas.
  • Capital to build: a new capital at Amaravati had to be built from scratch, adding to investment needs.

2. Resource gap

  • 2014-15 deficit: the Centre released ₹10,460.87 crore as the revenue-deficit grant for that year only in May 2023.
  • Finance Commission grants: the 14th FC gave revenue-deficit grants of ₹22,113 crore (2015-20), and the 15th FC continued them.
  • No special category status: instead, a Special Assistance Measure (2016) under which the Centre repays externally aided project loans signed in 2015-20.
  • Backward areas: seven backward districts of Rayalaseema and north coastal Andhra got development grants of ₹50 crore each a year, with ₹1,400 crore released in four instalments by March 2020.
  • Debt: liabilities of 33.3% of GSDP (2023-24 BE) and 36% (2026-27 BE), plus off-budget corporation borrowings (₹86,260 crore by March 2021, CAG).
  • Unfinished division: the division of Schedule IX and X institutions is still incomplete, keeping some assets and liabilities in dispute.

3. Steps taken to mobilise resources

  • Own revenue: GST compliance through data analytics, revised land registration values, and mining and excise reforms (new liquor policy, 2024).
  • Central support: Polavaram as a national project (Sec. 90), Amaravati funding, the steel plant package and 50-year interest-free capital loans under the Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI).
  • EAPs and PPPs: World Bank, AIIB and NDB projects, and Bhogapuram airport on a DBFOT basis.
  • Land and investment: Amaravati land pooling, asset monetisation, and the State Investment Promotion Board under the 2024 industrial policies.

Closing the gap durably needs higher own-tax effort, quality capital spending over committed spending, and full delivery of the Act's promises.
g1m-2023-p4-4a:
Goods and Services TaxInput tax creditGST CouncilEase of doing business

The Goods and Services Tax (GST), launched on 1 July 2017 under the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, is a destination-based, multi-stage tax on the supply of goods and services with seamless input tax credit. The Centre levies CGST and the States SGST (Art. 246A), IGST covers inter-State supply (Art. 269A), and the GST Council (Art. 279A) recommends rates. It subsumed 17 taxes and 13 cesses.

1. Key features

  • Dual GST: the Centre and States tax the same supply concurrently; since tax follows consumption, consuming States gain.
  • GST Council: chaired by the Union Finance Minister; decisions need three-fourths of the weighted votes, with the Centre holding one-third and the States two-thirds, a model of cooperative federalism.
  • Exclusions: alcohol for human consumption is outside GST, and five petroleum products stay outside until the Council decides.
  • Rates: since 'GST 2.0' (22 September 2025), two main slabs of 5% and 18%, plus 40% on sin and luxury goods.

2. Steps to facilitate trade and ease of doing business

  • Small taxpayers: a ₹40 lakh registration threshold for goods, a composition scheme up to ₹1.5 crore turnover, and quarterly returns with monthly payment (QRMP, 2021).
  • Technology: the GST Network, auto-populated returns (GSTR-2B), e-way bills (2018) and e-invoicing (2020, now for turnover above ₹5 crore) cut physical checks and fake invoicing.
  • Exporters: zero-rating, exports under a Letter of Undertaking without paying tax, and automated IGST refunds through ICEGATE.
  • Trust and disputes: higher prosecution thresholds and decriminalisation, an amnesty waiving interest and penalty on 2017-20 demands, and the GST Appellate Tribunal (operational from September 2025).
  • GST 2.0: fewer slabs and classification disputes, registration within three working days for low-risk applicants, and 90% provisional refunds for inverted duty structures.

3. Concerns that remain

  • Incomplete base: petroleum products and electricity outside GST break the input-credit chain for many industries.
  • Litigation: classification and refund disputes remain frequent despite the Appellate Tribunal.
  • Federal autonomy: States have given up most independent taxing powers and rely on the Council's consensus.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh enacted the APGST Act, 2017. As a consumption-heavy State it gains from the destination principle, and GST compensation protected its revenue until June 2022.

GST has built a common national market; bringing in petroleum and keeping rates stable would make it a truly 'Good and Simple Tax'.
g1m-2023-p4-4b:
15th Finance CommissionFiscal consolidationFiscal deficitDebt anchor

Fiscal consolidation means steadily reducing deficits and debt to sustainable levels. The 15th Finance Commission (Chair: N.K. Singh; award period 2021-26) laid down a gradual path after COVID-19, when the Centre's fiscal deficit had hit 9.2% of GDP (2020-21), balancing support for recovery with the need to restore sustainability.

1. Recommendations of the 15th FC

  • Centre's fiscal deficit: 6.0% of GDP in 2021-22, falling to 4.0% by 2025-26.
  • States' fiscal deficit: 4% of GSDP (2021-22), 3.5% (2022-23) and 3% (2023-26), with an extra 0.5% of GSDP for power-sector reforms (2021-25).
  • Debt and FRBM: reduce debt at both levels, and set up a high-powered inter-governmental group to review the FRBM Act and draft a new framework.
  • Off-budget borrowings: stop them, or disclose them fully in budget documents.
  • Revenue and spending: raise the tax-GDP ratio through better GST and income-tax administration, and improve the quality of spending.

2. Progress at the Centre

  • Deficit path: the fiscal deficit fell from 9.2% (2020-21) to 4.4% (2025-26 RE) and is budgeted at 4.3% for 2026-27. The government's own target of 'below 4.5% by 2025-26' was met, though not the FC's 4% path.
  • New anchor: from 2026-27 the Centre targets debt-to-GDP of 50±1% by March 2031; central debt is 56.1% (2025-26 RE) and 55.6% (2026-27 BE). This follows the N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee (2017), which preferred debt as the main anchor.
  • Transparency: food-subsidy borrowing from the National Small Savings Fund was brought on budget in 2020-21.
  • Quality: capital spending has risen to ₹12.2 lakh crore (2026-27), but interest absorbs nearly two-fifths of revenue receipts and a revenue deficit persists.

3. Present situation in the States

  • Aggregate: the States' combined deficit is near 3% of GDP, but several States are stressed by freebies, old-pension revival and discom losses.
  • Borrowing discipline: off-budget borrowings by State entities serviced from the budget now count against States' borrowing limits, which some States see as a curb on autonomy.
  • AP angle: Andhra Pradesh budgets a fiscal deficit of 3.8% and a revenue deficit of 1.1% of GSDP, with liabilities at 36% of GSDP (2026-27 BE), so its room for new borrowing is limited.

4. Assessment

The direction is right: deficits are falling while capital spending has risen. But the debt level is still well above the FRBM ideal, interest crowds out development spending, and consolidation has leaned on spending control more than on higher tax buoyancy.

Consolidation is on track at the Centre; sustainability now needs higher tax buoyancy, better spending quality and stricter State-level discipline.
g1m-2023-p4-5a:
Budgetary policyReallocation of resourcesSocial servicesAP Budget 2023-24

Budgetary policy uses taxes, spending, borrowing and transfers to steer resources where markets alone would not send them. In Musgrave's terms it performs the allocation, distribution and stabilisation functions. For a State like Andhra Pradesh, which carries most social-sector responsibilities under the Seventh Schedule, the budget is the main instrument of human development.

1. Importance of budgetary policy in reallocation

  • Correcting market failures: the budget supplies public and merit goods such as education, health and sanitation, which markets under-provide.
  • Redistribution: progressive taxes, subsidies and direct benefit transfers move resources to the poor, women and weaker sections.
  • Regional and sectoral balance: spending can be steered to lagging regions (Rayalaseema, north coastal and tribal areas) and to priority sectors such as irrigation and MSMEs.
  • Growth: capital spending builds future capacity, while revenue spending sustains consumption and human capital.
  • Stabilisation: higher spending in downturns and restraint in booms smooth the cycle, though this is mainly a Union role.

2. Social services in AP Budget 2023-24 (₹2,79,279 crore; fiscal deficit 3.8% of GSDP)

  • Welfare of SC, ST, BC and minorities: ₹51,292 crore, 19.8% of spending against a States' average of 3.5% (PRS); sub-plans of ₹20,000 crore (SC), ₹6,929 crore (ST) and ₹38,605 crore (BC).
  • Direct benefit transfers: ₹54,228 crore across 22 schemes, including YSR Pension Kanuka (₹21,434 crore) and YSR Aasara for SHG women (₹6,700 crore).
  • Education: ₹32,658 crore (12.6%, below the 14.8% States' average), including Mana Badi Nadu-Nedu school upgrades.
  • Health, nutrition and housing: health ₹16,207 crore; social welfare and nutrition ₹11,230 crore, including YSR Sampoorna Poshana (₹1,073 crore); housing ₹5,600 crore (Pedalandariki Illu). Rural development received ₹16,159 crore.

3. Assessment

  • Strengths: strongly redistributive and women-centred; DBT reduced leakages and middlemen.
  • Weaknesses: committed spending and DBT left little for capital outlay, and education stayed below the States' average.
  • Missing link: outlays were tracked more than outcomes such as learning levels, anaemia or employment.

4. Latest trend (AP Budget 2026-27, ₹3.32 lakh crore)

NTR Bharosa pensions (formerly YSR Pension Kanuka) get ₹27,719 crore; Thalliki Vandanam (replacing Amma Vodi) ₹8,456 crore; education, sports and culture ₹35,673 crore; and health ₹19,630 crore. Capital outlay rises by 47%, signalling a shift towards investment alongside welfare.

Budgets should balance welfare with human-capital and physical investment, and track outcomes, not just outlays.
g1m-2023-p4-5b:
Gender budgetingChild budgetingGender Budget StatementOutcome budgeting

Gender budgeting applies a gender lens to the whole budget cycle, from planning to audit, tracking how much spending reaches women and girls and with what effect; it began with Australia's women's budget (1984). Child budgeting tracks spending on children (0-18) for health, education, development and protection. Neither is a separate budget: both are analytical statements within the main budget.

1. Gender and child budgeting in India

  • Gender Budget Statement: carried in the Union Budget since 2005-06, with Part A (schemes 100% for women), Part B (30-99%) and, since 2024-25, Part C (below 30%).
  • Gender budget cells: set up in Union ministries to review schemes and spending from a gender angle.
  • Child budget: the Union has published a statement on allocations for children since 2008-09.
  • Purpose: both make the budget accountable for those who have little voice in it.

2. Does Andhra Pradesh follow them?

Yes. Andhra Pradesh has presented separate Gender Budget and Child Budget statements since 2021-22, counting the full cost of exclusive schemes and a beneficiary share of general ones.

  • Gender Budget 2023-24: about ₹77,914 crore (roughly 28% of the budget): Part A ₹31,826 crore (PMAY-U housing, YSR Cheyutha, Aasara, Amma Vodi) and Part B ₹46,089 crore (pensions, Rythu Bharosa, rice subsidy).
  • Child Budget 2023-24: about ₹20,593 crore (₹16,748 crore in 2021-22), mostly education (Nadu-Nedu, Samagra Shiksha, Vidya Deevena) and nutrition (ICDS, Sampoorna Poshana).
  • Latest: the statements continue (for example 2025-26) with renamed schemes, such as Thalliki Vandanam in place of Amma Vodi, along with Stree Shakti free bus travel for women (from August 2025).

3. Evaluation

  • Strengths: greater transparency; women are the main recipients of DBT; house-site pattas are issued in women's names.
  • Weaknesses: Part B inflates totals by apportioning general schemes (pensions, rice subsidy) on assumptions; there are no gender audits or outcome indicators; child protection gets little (Mission Vatsalya about ₹118 crore).
  • Outcomes lag: NFHS-5 (2019-21) found 58.8% of AP women anaemic and 31.2% of under-five children stunted.
  • Process gaps: the statements are compiled after allocations are decided, so they rarely shape priorities, and local bodies do not yet prepare their own.

AP follows both in form; in substance it should move from accounting to outcome budgeting, with sex- and age-disaggregated data, gender audits and local-level gender budgeting.
g1m-2023-p4-6a:
Differentiated bankingSmall Finance BanksPayments BanksDigital banking

Differentiated banking means licensing specialised, niche banks with limited activities, rather than only full-service universal banks. Following the Nachiket Mor Committee (2014), the RBI gave in-principle licences to 11 payments banks and 10 small finance banks in 2015 to reach the unbanked and underserved at low cost. Together with digital rails, they are the backbone of India's financial inclusion strategy.

1. Scope for financial inclusion

  • Small Finance Banks: lend to small farmers, micro enterprises and the unorganised sector, with minimum capital of ₹200 crore, 75% priority-sector lending and at least half of loans up to ₹25 lakh. Licensing is on tap since 2019; many grew out of microfinance institutions and brought their village reach into regulated banking.
  • Payments Banks: accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer and offer payments and remittances but cannot lend; India Post Payments Bank uses the postal network for doorstep service.
  • Complementary lenders: RRBs, cooperative banks, NBFC-MFIs and MUDRA loans fill the remaining gaps in rural and micro credit.
  • Limits: thin margins, risky small-ticket loans and payments banks' reliance on fees; several payments-bank licensees gave up their licences.

2. Potential of digital banking

  • JAM base: over 55 crore Jan Dhan accounts with Aadhaar e-KYC give almost every household an account.
  • UPI: about 20 billion transactions a month (2025), with UPI 123PAY for feature phones and credit lines on UPI.
  • Last mile: Aadhaar-enabled payments (AePS), business correspondents and 75 Digital Banking Units (2022) serve villages without branches.
  • Credit: Account Aggregators and the Unified Lending Interface allow cash-flow-based, collateral-free loans to MSMEs and farmers.
  • Result: the RBI's Financial Inclusion Index rose to 67.0 (March 2025).

3. Challenges

  • Skills and access: low digital literacy and patchy connectivity in remote areas.
  • Safety: rising cyber fraud and mis-selling erode trust; data protection depends on the DPDP Act 2023.
  • Gender gap: only 33% of women had ever used the internet (NFHS-5).
  • Usage: many accounts stay dormant, so access has not always meant use.

AP angle: Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats, SHG women working as banking correspondents and Stree Nidhi carry digital services to villages; under 'One State-One RRB' its four RRBs became the Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank (sponsored by Union Bank of India) from 1 May 2025.

Differentiated banks plus digital rails can deliver 'phygital' inclusion; the focus must now shift from accounts to usage, credit and consumer protection.
g1m-2023-p4-6b:
Women entrepreneurshipCollateral gapCare burdenCredit and market access

Women own only about one-fifth of MSMEs (NSS 73rd round) and 13.76% of establishments (Sixth Economic Census).
